item.title: Birefringence Breaks Symmetry-Protected Fluorescence Trapping in Laser-Cooled Crystals
item.description:
Total internal reflection traps light inside high-index emitters, and in laser-cooled crystals the trapped fluorescence limits how far purification lowers the parasitic heat load. The symmetry of the crystal shape is known to govern this trapping. Here we show that the dielectric tensor supplies a second, intrinsic symmetry, and we unify the geometric and dielectric symmetries in a single conservation law. A fluorescence photon stays trapped when every facet operation conserves a wave-vector component that keeps it inside total internal reflection. Mirror facets of a cuboid conserve three components and trap 17.2% of all directions. Brewster end facets, or mode conversion between ordinary and extraordinary waves at facets containing the optic axis of uniaxial Yb:YLF, leave one component and reduce the trapped set to a universal shell of 3.45% of directions. Sub-degree misorientation of the optic axis, subnanometer facet roughness or an asymmetric cut releases this shell, and the release rate determines how strongly purification lowers parasitic loss. Released Yb:YLF crystals keep nearly linear purity leverage at 77 K and tolerate about ten times more cold background and up to 240 times more facet absorption than the same crystals with mode-conserving reflection. Birefringence releases trapped light on the smoothest facets, where surface absorption is lowest. Crystal symmetry, set jointly by shape and dielectric tensor, thereby becomes a design parameter for optical refrigeration toward liquid-nitrogen temperature and for uniaxial scintillators, light-emitting diodes and other facet-bounded emitters that trap light by total internal reflection.

Daqian Bian, Yuzhi Xu

item.title: Multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential for the energetics and finite temperature structure of Pt surfaces and nanoparticles
item.description:
Accurate accounting of exposed facets and surface sites is central to understanding metal nanoparticle catalysts, but modelling their structure at finite temperatures is computationally expensive. We benchmark the universal interatomic potential UMA (Universal Model for Atoms, Open Catalyst 2020 task) against Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional theory (PBE-DFT) for Pt. UMA underestimates the surface energies of all 13 facets by 11-17 % and the excess energies of 28 differently shaped nanoparticles, each containing less than 500 atoms, most strongly for small particles. We distill UMA into a compact Deep Potential model by pre-training on UMA labelled bulk and slab data, then fine-tune it on a small PBE-DFT dataset that includes nanoparticles. The resulting multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential (MF-MLIP) gives a surface-energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.8 meV Å−2, 21 % lower than a DFT only model trained on the same data. On six nanoparticles, the MF-MLIP improves force accuracy over UMA, reducing the force RMSE by 29-52 %, with the largest gains at surface, edge and vertex atoms. Molecular dynamics at 500 K shows Pt(111) retaining its termination while Pt(100) and Pt(110) change strongly. At 500-700 K, the nanoparticles lose vertex sites and gain edge sites, and some restructure away from their ideal shapes. On the same CPU hardware, the MF-MLIP runs molecular dynamics simulations 60-100 times faster than UMA.

Noor Aldin Alzghoul, Wo Bin Bae, Jun Hee Jang, Aditya Dilip Lele

item.title: Designing Alloying Interlayers for Metal Anodes in Batteries: Does Nanostructuring Improve Reversibility?
item.description:
Metal anodes have been extensively explored as candidates for high-energy rechargeable batteries. However, uncontrolled electrodeposition of metals such as Zn often produces porous, disconnected “dead” metal that limits reversibility. A common mitigation strategy is to introduce an alloying functional layer, which is in general assumed to perform better when nanostructured due to its increased specific surface area and the diffusion scaling relation 𝜏~ 𝐿 2 𝐷 ⁄ . Here, we directly interrogate how the characteristic feature size of an alloying interlayer governs reversibility, using Ag functional layers with building blocks at three representative length scales: 100 nm, a few μm, and 100 μm, approximately. Combining operando visualization with ex-situ structural characterization, we find that Ag layers composed of few-μm particles exhibit the highest Zn plating and stripping reversibility. Coarse, 100-μm Ag particles provide poor areal coverage, such that beneficial Ag–Zn alloying is confined to isolated regions and does not effectively regulate deposition. In contrast, nanostructured Ag reacts rapidly and nearly completely, transforming into bulk intermetallic phases with large volume change that crack and delaminate from the current collector. Few-μm Ag features, on the one hand, provide sufficient surface coverage to promote uniform nucleation; on the other, Ag particles at this few-μm length scale prevent excessive intermetallic conversion and the associated mechanical failure. These results challenge the conventional wisdom that nanostructured layers are inherently more effective and reveal a previously overlooked mesoscopic design window for alloying interlayers. By explicitly linking alloying-layer feature size to diffusion-controlled phase transformation, mesoscale mechanical stability, and electrochemical behavior, this work identifies surface topography as a key design parameter for stabilizing multivalent metal anodes of high-energy batteries.

Sydney C. Manning, J. X. Kent Zheng

item.title: Structural Description of Two-Dimensional Nanoscale Networks Using Graph Theory and Graph Growth Algorithms
item.description:
Nanostructured networks stand out among other nanostructures for their unique combinations of properties and easily scalable energy-efficient synthesis. Their structural organization is, however, difficult to describe using traditional approaches based on crystallinity. Although revealing distinct structural patterns, the nanoscale networks also have a substantial degree of randomness. Two-dimensional (2D) nanostructured networks self-assembled from nanoparticles present a unique opportunity to develop the methodology for structural description of such materials. We describe nanostructured networks as sets of nodes and edges with corresponding weights taking advantage of the mathematical apparatus of Graph Theory (GT). Being extracted from electron microscopy images, the GT descriptors readily identify nanoscale networks obtained under different chemical conditions. Also important is that among the prior studies the GT description of properties has been extensively discussed, while better understanding of adequate GT descriptors is lagging. All GT descriptors were found to be scale-dependent, with average nodal degree, centrality metrics, multi-fractal dimension, and Ollivier-Ricci curvature following smooth superlinear or sublinear trajectories over several thousands of nodes. Statistical analysis of topological and metric parameters of nodes and edges enables development of topometric graph growth algorithms (TOGGA) that capture the structural uniqueness of each nanoscale network. Similarly to the infinite tiling of unit cells in crystals, TOGGA models enabled the extrapolation of nanoscale network structure, commensurate with both micro- and macroscale samples over 10 million nodes and 20 million edges. The predictions of electric transport through the networks comparable in size to experimental samples enable identification of knowledge gaps for rapid design of conductive nanoscale networks. TOGGA models can be used to map out experimentally realistic structures for inverse design of nanoscale networks.

Pavel Khavlyuk, Xiongye Xiao, Will Stephenson, Dickson Owuor, Chung Man Lim, Volodymyr Shamraienko, Wenbing Wu, Haiping Sun, Peiyu Zhang, Ronja Piehler, Rostyslav Lesyuk, Christian Klinke, Alexander Eychmüller, Paul Bogdan, Xiaoming Mao, Nicholas Kotov, Nicholas Alexander Kotov

item.title: Origin of the Difference between Kohn-Sham and ∆SCF Band gaps for Delocalized Electron–Hole Excitations in Hybrid-Functional Supercell Calculations
item.description:
We examine the relationship between ground-state generalized Kohn–Sham (GKS) band gaps and self-consistent ∆SCF excitation energies for delocalized electron–hole excitations in finite periodic supercells. For a vertical excitation at the undistorted ground-state geometry, these two quantities are expected to coincide when the promoted electron and hole remain Bloch-like. This is mostly true with semilocal functionals, but not with hybrid functionals for which the difference increases linearly with the fraction of exact exchange. The origin of this difference is derived from two equivalent viewpoints: the total-energy change associated with the ∆SCF excitation and the occupation-dependent orbital gap shift arising from the self-consistent potential response. The residual energy arises from the orbital-dependent exact-exchange selfenergy associated with the electron-hole pair and decreases approximately as 1/N

Mingxue Fu, Arghya Bhowmik, Juan Maŕıa Garćıa-Lastra

item.title: First-principles data for solid-solution Nb–Zr, Ta–Zr, and V–Zr binary alloys with body-centered-cubic structures
item.description:
We present three open-access datasets containing density functional theory (DFT) calculations for refractory solid-solution binary alloys niobium–zirconium (NbZr), tantalum–zirconium (TaZr), and vanadium–zirconium (VZr) in 128-atom body-centered-cubic (BCC) supercells. These datasets extend our previously published first-principles collections for NbTa, NbV, TaV, and NbTaV alloys and were generated with the same automated high-throughput workflow based on the Vienna Ab-Initio Simulation Package (VASP). For each of the three NbZr, TaZr, and VZr systems, we uniformly sample 31 chemical compositions across the full composition range in 4-atom increments. For every composition we construct 100 distinct disordered atomic configurations by randomizing the element assignments on the BCC lattice sites. All structures are fully relaxed, and the released data include complete input files, detailed VASP outputs for each relaxation stage, and derived physical quantities such as ground-state formation energy and root mean-squared displacement (RMSD) relative to an ideal BCC reference. These Zr-containing binaries are motivated by our earlier demonstration that graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on binary NbTa, NbV, and TaV data can interpolate formation enthalpies and structural descriptors in ternary NbTaV alloys while dramatically reducing the required number of ternary DFT calculations. The new NbZr, TaZr, and VZr datasets increase the diversity of available binary training data, in particular in systems with larger size mismatch and stronger lattice distortion due to Zr, and are intended to support the development of transferable machine learning (ML) interatomic models for accelerated exploration of high-dimensional multicomponent alloy spaces.

Massimiliano Lupo Pasini, German Samolyuk, Jong Youl Choi, David Rogers, Ying Yang

item.title: Metalsurfer: Fast Generation of Realistic Substrate-Adsorbate Interfaces
item.description:
Realistic adsorbate–substrate geometries are essential for meaningful electronic-structure calculations at interfaces, yet constructing them remains slow and generally ad hoc for bulky molecules, high coverages, and irregular surfaces. This challenge limits systematic exploration of adsorption configurations across many problems in catalysis, surface chemistry, and materials design. We introduce metalsurfer, a Python package that generates density functional theory (DFT)-ready interface models from simplified molecular input line-entry system (SMILES) strings and a substrate. The workflow combines chemistry-aware, CPU-parallel placement enumeration with TorchSim GPU-batched relaxation under a machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP), molecular integrity filters, sequential coverage growth, and optional Bayesian acquisition. We demonstrate these capabilities on three chemically distinct systems. For camphor on Cu(111), a ∼1.2 h search recovers neighbors to all eight published weak-adsorption minima and provides a set of plausible basins for refinement. For bipyridine on defected Au(111), offline fixed-batch replays on saved saturation pools show that probability-of-improvement acquisition identifies the first committed motif much faster than random sampling. Transfer from earlier coverage steps also accelerates later searches, with a trust gate that can fall back to a cold model if the prior fails current-step validation. For CO/Pt(111), fixed-coverage n-tuplet searches locate all four ordered adlayers reported in the literature. In each case, a few hours of GPU screening produce a compact shortlist for DFT refinement. metalsurfer thus provides a practical route through the combinatorial problem of interface construction.

Jorge Gonzalo, Jorge Felez, Julen Munarriz, Ruben Laplaza

item.title: Paper2CIF: An AI Agent for Reconstructing Atomistic Models to Discover Structure-Reactivity Relationships
item.description:
Reinterpreting published chemical findings requires explicit atomic structures that connect experimental observations with reactivity. Here we report Paper2CIF, an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that reconstructs sample-specific atomic structures from published chemical evidence for structure-reactivity relationship investigations. Across 171 interdisciplinary articles, Paper2CIF achieves 97.08% phase identification accuracy and 91.23% final structural accuracy, with correct structures satisfying all applicable reported constraints, including composition, site occupancy, and local coordination. Calculations on reconstructed BiVO4 structures reveal distortion-dependent spatial contributions to the transition dipole, guiding targeted synthesis toward enhanced near-edge photon conversion. The resulting BiVO4-based Z-scheme pair exhibits a 3.47-fold increase in apparent quantum yield from 4.51% to 15.64% at 475 nm, compared with a 1.03-fold increase from 18.51% to 19.02% at 365 nm. The solar-to-hydrogen efficiency increases from 0.969% to 1.448% for overall water splitting. Paper2CIF establishes atomic reconstruction as a common basis for deriving chemical mechanisms from published evidence and translating them into experimentally testable principles for materials synthesis.

Qixin Zhou, Yonghang Yue, Wenjie Guo, Yongfa Zhu, Yan Guo

item.title: Memory-Augmented Generative Design of Octahedral Co(II) Complexes with Targeted Zero-Field Splitting
item.description:
The discovery of coordination complexes with targeted magnetic anisotropy remains challenging because the enormous chemical space of ligands and coordination environments makes propertydirected molecular design difficult to achieve by conventional screening. Here, we introduce a memoryaugmented generative framework for the inverse design of octahedral Co(II) complexes with targeted zero-field splitting (ZFS). A chemically curated dataset of ~6000 Co(II) complexes, was used to establish a broad electronic-structure landscape spanning positive and negative ZFS regimes. Building on this chemical space, a generative strategy was developed in which ligand structures are iteratively mutated, recombined, and selected according to their predicted magnetic properties, while an elitememory mechanism preserves high-performing molecular motifs and guides subsequent generations toward increasingly favorable candidates. This enables targeted exploration of ligand combinations and coordination environments associated with large negative ZFS while simultaneously controlling rhombicity. The generated complexes were subjected to independent CASSCF calculations, including spin–orbit coupling, to directly validate their magnetic properties. Notably, the generative framework identified candidates with strongly enhanced axial anisotropy, including a representative complex exhibiting D ≈ −223 cm-1 after ab initio validation. The validated candidates reproduced the targeted ZFS with deviations of approximately 15–18 cm-1. These results establish a generative, memory-guided route from ligand design to electronically validated magnetic complexes, providing a practical strategy for discovering previously unexplored Co(II) molecular magnets and advancing molecular-magnet design from screening toward property-directed generation.

Rajanikanta Rana, Aditya Choudhary, Abhijeet Biswas, Subodh Bhalchandra Rawool, Gopalan Rajaraman
